quotes.text: A web hook is an HTTP request sent automatically when something happens. You don't ask for it. The server just pushes it to you.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Gives a crisp, beginner-friendly definition of a webhook.

quotes.text: Acknowledge immediately and process asynchronously. Your endpoint should validate the client state, accept the notification, and return it 200 or 202 responses as fast as possible.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States the core best practice for reliable webhook endpoints.

quotes.text: Use web hooks to tell you when something changed. Then use Delta query to find out exactly what changed.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarises the recommended webhook-plus-Delta-query integration pattern.

quotes.text: Web hooks give you speed and Delta query gives you reliability. Together, they're a powerful combination.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: Stop polling. Start listening. Web hooks let you move from constantly asking Microsoft Graph for updates to getting notified instantly when something changes.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

chapters.title: The polling problem and Graph throttling

takeaways: Polling Microsoft Graph wastes thousands of requests, still misses real-time changes and can push your app into throttling.
A Graph webhook needs a subscription with notification URL, resource, change type and expiration, plus a validation handshake that echoes the token as plain text.
Acknowledge notifications within seconds, process them asynchronously, renew subscriptions before they expire and use Delta query as a safety net for missed changes.
hook: Is your app still asking Microsoft Graph every few minutes whether anything has changed? This episode explains to Microsoft 365 developers how Graph webhooks replace polling with change notifications, how subscriptions and validation work, and why combining them with Delta query gives you integrations that are both fast and reliable.
